title: Step 2: what people say about each feature

steps.headline: Tapping a mark opens a popup with what we found and what people say, and you can give your own answer.
steps.changed: The small tip becomes a popup. "What we found" is the same AI answer and source as before. Under it, "What people say": everyone's answers so far ("3 people: 3 partly"), your Yes / Partly / No, a comment box once you've answered, and the comments with GitHub names.
steps.notice: People's answers show from the very first one, as you asked. Totals carry no names; comments do.
steps.risk: The votes and comments in these pictures are made-up samples; the real site starts at zero. Votes and comments need the server step before they work for real.

steps.headline: Once 5 people have answered, the table's mark shows their average, and the AI's answer is no longer shown.
steps.changed: The AI said reveal.js can't open PowerPoint files (✗). In this sample 7 people answered, 6 yes and 1 no, so the mark becomes ✓ and the popup says "Table shows: Yes". The "What we found" card goes, as you chose.
steps.notice: The community's view outweighs the AI's once enough people agree.
steps.risk: Other marks in the sample table also moved, because the made-up voters don't always agree with the AI. The average counts partly as half a yes, so 3 yes and 2 no shows as partly.

steps.path: Interface design → Compare → a blank dot, signed out
steps.headline: A "not checked yet" dot can now be tapped, so anyone can give the first answer.
steps.changed: Before, the dot did nothing. Now it opens the same popup, with one card: "Nobody has checked this yet. Be the first." Signed out, it says answering needs a GitHub sign-in; pressing an answer opens sign-in.
steps.notice: The blanks (about 1 in 5 paid-app answers) can be filled by people who use the app.
steps.risk: The dot looks the same as before, so people may not guess it's tappable; the key under the table now says "Tap a mark to see its source or give your answer".

steps.path: Interface design → Compare → Penpot, signed in as Penpot's developer, Edit
steps.headline: A project's verified developer gets their own "From the developer" answer, kept apart from everyone else's.
steps.changed: A "From the developer" card shows their answer, note and name. Their own Edit opens Yes / Partly / No, a note and Save. Their answer isn't counted in "What people say", and they can't also vote there.
steps.notice: Maintainers have a separate voice, as you described; it never tips the average.
steps.risk: Only developers who already claimed their project ("Tag my project") see this.

steps.path: Presentations → Compare → tap a mark, on a phone
steps.headline: On a phone the popup slides up from the bottom, like the site's other popups.
steps.changed: Same content; the Yes / Partly / No buttons fill the width so they're easy to tap.
steps.risk: Long comment lists scroll inside the sheet.

steps.path: Penpot → Listed in → "Does Penpot do this job?" → Not really
steps.headline: Answering "Not really" now asks what stopped it, the comment you approved in October when the boards were removed.
steps.changed: A small popup: one box, "Optional. Shown with your GitHub name.", Send (greyed until you type) and Skip. Your "Not really" is already saved either way.
steps.notice: Developers and visitors learn why a project falls short, not just that it does.

steps.headline: Once someone has said what stopped it, a small button under the score opens what they wrote.
steps.changed: "1 said what stopped it" under the score; tapping it lists the comments with names. The score also now shows counts from the first answer ("2 yes · 1 not really") instead of "not enough for a score".
steps.notice: Something useful shows even with one answer, as you asked.
